title: Variations between American States Maternal Mortality Data and Its Consequences on National Metrics
abstract: Since 2007, the United States has not produced an official maternal mortality statistic. As health work uses metrics as one of its main tools for policies and practices, the lack of an official number is a point of concern for those that work on maternal child health. To understand the potential difficulties in producing a national metric, this research project focused on how states data collection can hinder the creation of official numbers. This meant that the date methods like terminology used, following of CDC and/or WHO guidelines, frequency that maternal death records are collected, that each state used was collected and compared. The research found that producing one national metric would be very difficult due to the different methods including timelines and definitions that each state follows for their individual data production. Consequently, even if the US produced data, the metric would have many limitations and not be an accurate or precise number that would be most beneficial for policy making. While the lack of an official maternal mortality metric from the US for over the past 10 years may seem like a mistake and lack of political interest in the field, it can also be seen as saving resources by not producing official numbers that would be an inadequate representation of maternal health in the US. Furthermore, this project showcases that producing a valuable maternal mortality metric depends on more than the work of federal agencies as the lack of organization and inconsistency between states prevents the National Center for Health Statistics from having useable information for the metric.
